subject: 동물의 도덕적 지위
title: The moral standing of animals
content: Almost everyone accepts that gratuitous cruelty to animals is morally wrong, and yet most people also accept practices that cause animals considerable suffering. Moral philosophy has pressed on this inconsistency for several decades, because the arguments it has produced are harder to dismiss than the comfortable middle position suggests. The central question is what gives a creature moral standing at all, and every answer proposed has consequences that reach beyond the case it was designed to settle. One tradition locates that standing in the capacity to suffer, holding that a being whose experience can go better or worse has interests which any adequate ethics must weigh. This account explains the wrongness of cruelty directly, and it therefore extends moral consideration to any creature with the relevant capacity. Its critics object that weighing such interests across species requires comparisons nobody knows how to make, and they add that the principle proves too much if it is applied consistently. A second tradition ties moral standing to rational agency, so that only beings who can recognize obligations may hold rights. That view draws a sharp line, although it also excludes human infants and the severely impaired, which few of its defenders accept. Attempts to repair it by appealing to species membership are widely regarded as arbitrary, since the argument then rests on a biological fact rather than on any moral one. The debate persists because each account preserves a judgment we are unwilling to give up while denying another we hold just as firmly.

subject: 인쇄술 이전의 책 유통
title: How books circulated before printing
content: Before printing, every copy of a book was made by hand, and this fact shaped what could be read and by whom. A single manuscript required months of a trained scribe's labour together with the skins of many animals, so books were expensive in a way that is hard to imagine now. Yet medieval Europe was not without books, and the number in circulation grew steadily across the centuries that preceded the press. Understanding how requires attention to the institutions that carried the cost. Monasteries copied texts as an act of devotion, and their libraries lent volumes to one another so that a house could obtain an exemplar without buying it. Universities developed a different arrangement, dividing an approved text into sections that students hired and copied in parallel, which shortened the time a book was out of circulation. Booksellers in the larger towns kept stocks of the works their customers most often wanted and commissioned copies against orders. Each of these systems solved the same problem in a different way, and each produced its own characteristic errors in the texts that survive. The press did not create the demand it served. It arrived in a world where the machinery of copying, correcting, and lending was already elaborate, and its first products imitated manuscripts closely because that was what buyers expected. What changed was the cost of the twentieth copy rather than the first, and the consequences of that single change took a century to unfold.

subject: 약속은 왜 구속력을 갖는가
title: Why a promise binds
content: A promise seems to create an obligation out of nothing more than words, and moral philosophy has long found this puzzling. Before I speak I am free to act as I choose; afterwards I am bound, though nothing about the world has altered except that a sentence was uttered. Any adequate account must explain how mere utterance generates a genuine moral requirement, and several rival explanations have been offered. The simplest appeals to consequences. Promising is a useful practice, trust makes cooperation possible, and breaking promises erodes the practice for everyone. This explains why the institution has value, but critics argue that it explains the wrong thing. It gives me a reason to keep my promise when doing so protects the practice, and no reason at all when my breach would go unnoticed, which is not how the obligation feels or how we judge such cases. A second account holds that promising creates a right in the person promised, so that breaking the promise wrongs that particular individual rather than the institution. This matches our judgments more closely, since we think the injured party is owed an apology and has the standing to release me. What it does not explain is how a right can be conjured by speech, and defenders answer that the power to bind oneself is itself part of what it is to be a moral agent. The puzzle remains, but it has been located precisely.

subject: 로마 콘크리트와 건축의 규모
title: Roman concrete and the scale of ancient building
content: The ancient Romans built vaults and domes of a size that would not be equalled for more than a thousand years, and the material that made this possible was concrete. Their formula combined lime, volcanic ash, and rubble, and it set through a chemical reaction rather than by drying, which meant it could cure under water and in the interior of a mass too thick for air to reach. Modern analysis has shown that the reaction continued for years, and that mineral crystals formed within the cracks in a way that sealed them. What the material permitted was a change in how a building was conceived. Cut stone must be assembled from pieces whose shapes are decided in advance, so the form follows what a mason can carve and lift. Concrete is poured into a mould, and the mould can take any shape that carpenters can build. Ancient architects accordingly began to design interiors as volumes of enclosed space rather than as arrangements of supports, and the great domed halls of the period are the result. Supply mattered as much as chemistry. The volcanic ash that gave the mixture its strength came from particular regions, and it had to be shipped in quantity to wherever a major work was rising. When the administrative system that organized such shipments broke down, the technique was not so much forgotten as rendered impossible, and later builders returned to stone because the ancient supply lines no longer existed.

subject: 덕과 규칙 — 두 윤리의 대립
title: Virtue and rule in moral theory
content: Modern moral philosophy has largely asked what makes an action right, and it has answered with rules: maximize good consequences, or act only on principles you could will to be universal. An older tradition asked a different question, namely what makes a person good, and answered in terms of virtues such as courage, honesty, and justice. The two approaches are not simply different emphases, because each treats the other's central concept as derivative. Rule-based theories have a clear advantage in hard cases. When two people disagree about what to do, a principle can be stated, examined, and applied, whereas an appeal to what a virtuous person would do seems to presuppose the answer. Defenders of virtue reply that this advantage is illusory, since every rule requires judgment in its application, and judgment is precisely what a virtue is. Knowing that honesty is required does not tell you whether this particular silence counts as deception. The virtue tradition also claims to explain something rules leave out. A person who does the right thing while resenting it every moment has met the requirement without being good, and most of us think the difference matters morally. Rule theorists answer that motives can be evaluated by rules as well, and that the truth about right action should not depend on who happens to be acting. The disagreement runs deep because it concerns what ethics is for.

subject: 거짓말이 언제나 그른가
title: Whether lying is always wrong
content: Few moral rules command wider assent than the prohibition on lying, and few are more often broken by people who accept them. The interesting question is not whether lying is generally wrong, which almost everyone grants, but whether the wrongness admits of exception, and moral philosophy has produced a striking range of answers. One position holds that the prohibition is absolute. To lie is to use another person's rational capacity as an instrument against their own judgment, and no consequence can justify treating a person that way. Defenders accept the notorious implication that one may not lie even to a murderer seeking a victim, arguing that the truth of what follows is not the liar's responsibility while the lie itself certainly is. Most philosophers find this conclusion a reason to reject the premise. The opposing view treats the wrongness of lying as real but defeasible, so that it can be outweighed when enough is at stake. This matches ordinary moral judgment, yet it raises a question about what the prohibition then amounts to. If a sufficiently good outcome licenses deception, the rule seems to collapse into a general instruction to do what is best, and the distinctive wrong of the lie disappears. A middle position holds that lying wrongs the person deceived even when it is justified overall, so that something is owed afterwards. This preserves both judgments, and it explains why justified deception still leaves a residue.

subject: 이슬람 세계의 학문 전승
title: Learning transmitted through the Islamic world
content: Much of ancient Greek science reached medieval Europe by way of Arabic, and the usual account of this passage calls it preservation, as though scholars in the Islamic world had merely stored texts until Europe was ready for them. The manuscripts themselves tell a different story. Translators worked from Greek and Syriac copies, but they also corrected, annotated, and argued with what they turned into Arabic, and the notes that gathered around a text often ran longer than the text itself. Ancient astronomy shows this clearly. Greek models predicted the planets well enough for their own purposes, yet centuries of watching the sky from new places exposed gaps, and scholars in the medieval Islamic world built geometric devices to close them. Those devices turn up later in European work, and how they travelled is still argued over. Medicine, optics, and algebra followed much the same path, each gaining a body of fresh results that the later European reading absorbed without always saying so. What made this possible was as much a matter of money as of talent. Libraries were endowed, copyists were paid, and scholars moved between cities across a region that shared one learned tongue. When a patron died or a centre declined, the work went on elsewhere, and the thread held because people could move. Calling the period a holding operation therefore misreads it, and it hides the point at which the ancient inheritance stopped being merely inherited.

subject: 미래 세대에 대한 의무
title: What we owe to future generations
content: We readily accept that our conduct can wrong people who are not yet born, and environmental ethics rests heavily on this judgment. Making the judgment precise, however, runs into a difficulty that moral philosophy has found remarkably stubborn. The people who will exist in the distant future depend on what we do now, since different policies lead to different individuals being conceived. A person born into a depleted world therefore cannot complain that our choices harmed her, because a different choice would have meant that she never existed at all. This result is unwelcome, and several responses have been attempted. One denies that harm requires a comparison with how the same individual would otherwise have fared, holding instead that we wrong people by bringing them into conditions below a certain threshold. Another shifts the moral focus from individuals to states of affairs, arguing that a worse world is worse whoever inhabits it, and that no identified victim is needed for the judgment to hold. Both moves have costs. The first requires an account of the threshold that does not simply restate the intuition it was meant to justify, and the second commits us to comparing populations of different sizes, which generates conclusions most people reject. The practical upshot is that our confidence about our obligations to the future exceeds our ability to explain them, and this gap is not merely academic when policies are defended by appeal to those obligations.

subject: 대항해 시대의 질병 교환
title: The exchange of disease across the ocean
content: When ships began crossing the Atlantic regularly, they carried far more than cargo and passengers, and the biological consequences reshaped two hemispheres within a century. Populations in the Americas had been separated from those of Eurasia and Africa for a very long time, and they therefore had no exposure to the diseases that centuries of dense settlement and close contact with livestock had made endemic across the older world. The result was mortality on a scale that historical demography still struggles to estimate. What made these epidemics so severe was less the virulence of any single disease than their arrival together and in succession. A community weakened by one outbreak met the next before it had recovered, and the deaths fell heavily on adults whose labour and knowledge the survivors depended on. Fields consequently went untended, and famine followed the epidemics as reliably as the epidemics had followed the ships. The exchange was not entirely one-directional, since diseases moved eastward as well, although the balance was overwhelmingly unequal. Historians now treat this exchange as a central fact of the period rather than as background to the political narrative. The conquests that followed were accomplished by small forces against societies already in collapse, and explanations that credit the technology or the tactics of the invaders account for far less of the outcome than the pathogens which had preceded them inland, often reaching communities that had never seen a ship.

subject: 규범은 사실에서 도출되는가
title: Deriving what ought to be from what is
content: A familiar principle in moral philosophy holds that no statement about what ought to be the case follows from statements about what is. Observing that a practice is widespread, or that it accords with our nature, tells us nothing by itself about whether it is right, and any argument that moves from the one to the other has smuggled in a premise it did not state. The principle has been enormously influential, and it is often treated as settling the matter. Its defenders point out how much bad reasoning it exposes. Appeals to what is natural, to what has always been done, or to what most people prefer all attempt exactly the forbidden move, and stating the missing premise usually reveals that it is doing all the work while being far less obvious than the conclusion. On this view the value of the principle lies in forcing arguments into the open. Critics reply that the gap is narrower than it appears. Some concepts seem to carry both descriptive and evaluative content at once, so that calling an act cruel both describes it and condemns it, and one cannot accept the description while rejecting the judgment. If such concepts exist, then facts stated using them do bear on what we ought to do. The dispute turns on whether these thick concepts can be separated into a neutral description plus an attitude, and that question has resisted a settled answer.

subject: 사적 소유의 정당화
title: Justifying private ownership
content: Ownership seems so basic that its justification is rarely examined, yet a claim of private property is a claim that everyone else may be excluded from something that was once open to all. Moral and political philosophy has therefore asked what could make such a claim legitimate, and the answers proposed differ sharply in what they permit. One classic argument holds that a person owns her own labour, and that mixing labour with an unowned thing extends that ownership to the thing itself. The argument has intuitive force, and it accounts for the sense that what one has made is one's own. Critics have pressed two objections that remain unanswered. It is unclear why mixing what I own with what I do not should give me the whole rather than lose me the labour, and the condition that enough be left for others is difficult to satisfy once resources are finite. A second argument abandons origins and looks to consequences, holding that private ownership is justified because it produces better outcomes than the alternatives. This avoids the puzzles about acquisition, but it makes property contingent on performance, so that a distribution which failed to deliver those outcomes would lose its justification entirely. A third approach grounds ownership in the requirements of freedom, arguing that a person cannot act on her own purposes without secure control over some external things. Each account justifies a different institution, which is why the disagreement is political as well as philosophical.

subject: 중세 온난기와 북방 정착
title: The medieval warm centuries and northern settlement
content: For several centuries in the medieval period, temperatures across the North Atlantic ran somewhat warmer than in the eras on either side, and the farms that spread north during this interval are often read as proof of what climate can do. Fields appeared in regions that had supported none before, sea ice drew back enough for regular voyages, and people settled at latitudes that later proved impossible to hold. When conditions turned, those settlements failed, and the sequence looks like a clean natural test. Closer study of the dug evidence has made the lesson less tidy. The northern colonies were never self-sufficient, since they leaned on trade with the regions they had left for iron, timber, and grain. That trade was open to events which had nothing to do with temperature, among them shifts in what European markets wanted and the breaking of the routes that carried it. Excavated middens show diets moving toward fish and seal long before the climate worsened, which suggests that farming had been marginal from early on. What ended these medieval settlements was therefore a mix in which cooling was one factor among several. Communities that changed how they fed themselves survived conditions that destroyed neighbours who did not, and the record accordingly supports a claim about weakness rather than a claim about weather. Climate set the terms; the arrangements each community had built decided the outcome.
